items.readable_text:
Content:
There is something interesting about the bases of a subspace, summarized in the theorem below:

Content:
> If the vector space [MATH: V] has a basis with [MATH: n] vectors, then any basis of [MATH: V] has exactly [MATH: n] vectors.

Content:
The number [MATH: n] of vectors in any basis of [MATH: V] is called the dimension of the space [MATH: V] and is denoted [MATH: \textrm{dim}(V).]

Content:
For example, consider the linear span below:
[MATH: [3; − 1]]

Content:
We know that, in order to find a basis of the span, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

Content:
[MATH: M|=[3|− 3|− 6; − 1|1|5]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (1)/(3)R_{1}; ∼[3|− 3|− 6; 0|0|3]]

Content:
We see that the matrix above has two pivot columns: the [MATH: 1]st and the [MATH: 3]rd columns. This tells us that
[MATH: \mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_3 \}] is a basis of [MATH: H.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathcal{B}] consists of two vectors, any basis of [MATH: H] will also have exactly two vectors. So, we have [MATH: \textrm{dim}(H)=2.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
There is something interesting about the bases of a subspace, summarized in the theorem below:

Content:
> If the vector space [MATH: V] has a basis with [MATH: n] vectors, then any basis of [MATH: V] has exactly [MATH: n] vectors.

Content:
The number [MATH: n] of vectors in any basis of [MATH: V] is called the dimension of the space [MATH: V] and is denoted [MATH: \textrm{dim}(V).]

Content:
For example, consider the linear span below:
[MATH: [3; − 1]]

Content:
We know that, in order to find a basis of the span, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

Content:
[MATH: M|=[3|− 3|− 6; − 1|1|5]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (1)/(3)R_{1}; ∼[3|− 3|− 6; 0|0|3]]

Content:
We see that the matrix above has two pivot columns: the [MATH: 1]st and the [MATH: 3]rd columns. This tells us that
[MATH: \mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_3 \}] is a basis of [MATH: H.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathcal{B}] consists of two vectors, any basis of [MATH: H] will also have exactly two vectors. So, we have [MATH: \textrm{dim}(H)=2.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Finite and Infinite-Dimensional Vector Spaces

Content:
As defined earlier, the dimension of a vector space [MATH: V] is the number of vectors in any basis of [MATH: V].

Content:
However, note that the definition above is only applicable if a vector space has at least one basis with a finite number of elements.

Content:
- If a vector space has a basis with a finite number of vectors, then it is called finite-dimensional.
- Otherwise, if there is no finite basis, the vector space is called infinite-dimensional.

Content:
In linear algebra, we mostly consider finite-dimensional vector spaces.

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding the Dimension of a Span by Inspection

[MATH: [1; 0; 0]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

[MATH: [1|1|1; 0|1|1; 0|0|0]]

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form. We see that the matrix above has two pivot columns: the [MATH: 1]st and the [MATH: 2]nd columns. This tells us that [MATH: \mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2 \}] forms a basis for our span.

Since [MATH: \mathcal{B}] consists of two vectors, any basis of our span will also have exactly two vectors. Therefore, the dimension of the span is [MATH: 2\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: [1; 0; 0]]
